soil-meth-046.title: Why nearby soil samples are not independent
soil-meth-046.text: Two soil samples taken a meter apart usually tell you more about each other than two taken kilometers apart. That is spatial autocorrelation: properties at nearby places vary together, positively or negatively, a core idea in {{ref:soil-meth-045}}. It creates a problem, because standard statistics assume independent observations, and nearby samples are not. Dependence also helps, since one location can predict another and you need not sample both. Heterogeneity limits that help: if the relation changes across space, a dependence cannot be trusted beyond a possibly small region. Moran's I, Geary's C and Getis's G are the classic statistics for measuring it.

soil-meth-048.title: Stratified sampling: sampling each group on its own
soil-meth-048.text: A field with a sandy ridge and a clay hollow is really two populations. Stratified sampling treats them that way. It partitions a population into subpopulations, called strata, and samples each stratum independently, for example by simple random sampling. The strata must be collectively exhaustive and mutually exclusive, so every element falls in exactly one. Done well, it reduces sampling error and improves precision. The estimation error is smaller when the standard deviation within strata is lower than the overall one, and the method ensures enough samples from strata of interest. Proportionate allocation samples each stratum in proportion to its size. Optimum allocation takes larger samples where variability is greatest, and Neyman allocation is one such strategy. One trap remains: combining sub-strata to reach adequate numbers can cause Simpson's paradox, in which trends disappear or reverse.

soil-meth-035.title: Compositional data: when only the ratios matter
soil-meth-035.text: A soil analysis that reports sand, silt and clay as percentages describes parts of a whole, and that changes the statistics. Compositional data are quantitative descriptions of the parts of some whole, conveying relative information. Proportions, percentages and ppm all count, and so do molar concentrations in chemistry and the mineral fractions of a rock in geology. John Aitchison defined them in 1982 as proportions of some whole. Mathematically they are points on a simplex. Closure divides each part by the total, so only the ratios between components carry information, and scaling by any positive constant changes nothing. A three-part composition is plotted on a ternary (barycentric) triangle, where its position shows the ratios of the three variables.

soil-meth-036.title: Log-ratio transformations for compositional data
soil-meth-036.text: Ordinary statistics break down on compositions, so analysts translate them first. Log-ratio transformations map compositions from the simplex into real space, where standard methods apply. These transformations build on {{ref:soil-meth-035}}. The additive log ratio takes logs of ratios to one arbitrarily chosen component. It is common in chemistry (pH) and in multinomial logistic regression, but it is not an isometry. The centred log ratio is an isomorphism and an isometry, though it forces a linear dependency, so the covariance matrix is singular. The isometric log ratio gives orthonormal coordinates in D-1 dimensions, built by Gram-Schmidt, singular-value decomposition or a bifurcating tree. A caution applies: the article argues that noise distorts compositions asymmetrically, so the isometric version can create artifacts in real data.

soil-meth-051.title: Soil survey intensity levels
soil-meth-051.text: How hard a surveyor looks decides how much a soil map can be trusted. Survey intensity levels grade how densely a conventional soil survey, described in {{ref:soil-meth-050}}, is checked in the field. Level 1, very detailed, needs one inspection per polygon, with foot traverses under 0.5 km apart, and is published at 1:5,000 at series level. Level 2, detailed, inspects over 90% of polygons with traverses 2 km apart, at 1:20,000. Level 3, reconnaissance, inspects 60-80% with traverses 4 km apart, at 1:50,000. Each step down in intensity trades checking for coverage.

soil-meth-044.title: Sampling design: the odds behind every sample
soil-meth-044.text: A sample is only as good as the rule that produced it. A sampling design specifies, for every possible sample, its probability of being drawn. It is written as a function P(S) giving the probability of drawing sample S, and Bernoulli sampling is one example. Designing a sample means defining the population, the sampling frame and the sampling unit. It also means choosing the margin of error to achieve and deciding how to balance sampling and non-sampling error.

soil-meth-052.title: Choosing where to sample for a digital soil map
soil-meth-052.text:
A digital soil map is only as good as the sites that train it. The aim of sampling design here is to select sites representative of the geographic area and of the soil-forming factors, the covariates, being modelled. Two families of design exist, building on {{ref:soil-meth-044}}.

Geometric designs work on the map. They include grid, simple random, stratified random, transect, cluster and nested sampling. Grid sampling places points at the centre of evenly spaced cells, and stratified random applies random sampling within strata, as in {{ref:soil-meth-048}}. Cluster sampling groups sites closely to cope with rough terrain, and nested sampling quantifies variability at different distances.

Feature-space designs work on the covariate values instead. Fuzzy k-means sampling minimises distance in covariate space. Conditioned Latin hypercube sampling (Minasny and McBratney, 2006) samples all covariates with one sample per stratum. An optimal design covers both geographic and feature space.

soil-meth-038.title: Fuzzy clustering: points that belong to several groups
soil-meth-038.text: Soils rarely fall neatly into one class, and fuzzy clustering admits it. Also called soft clustering, it lets each data point belong to more than one cluster. In hard clustering each point belongs to exactly one cluster. Fuzzy clustering instead gives each point a membership grade for every cluster, and points at a cluster's edge have lower grades. Fuzzy c-means, developed by Dunn in 1973 and improved by Bezdek in 1981, alternates computing membership-weighted centroids with updating each point's coefficients until they converge. A parameter m controls fuzziness: larger m gives fuzzier clusters, m near 1 reduces to k-means, and m is commonly set to 2 without other knowledge. Like k-means, it finds only a local minimum that depends on the initial weights.

soil-meth-040.title: Latin hypercube sampling: one point per slice
soil-meth-040.text: Picture a chess board with rooks placed so that none can attack another. Latin hypercube sampling works the same way. It is a statistical method for generating a near-random sample of parameter values from a multidimensional distribution. The range of each variable is split into M equally probable intervals, and M points are placed so that each interval of every variable holds exactly one point. It needs no more samples for more variables, and samples can be taken in sequence while remembering which cells were already used. Unlike plain random sampling, the number of points must be chosen beforehand. In return, every subspace is sampled with equal density.

soil-meth-049.title: Uncertainty quantification: how sure is the model?
soil-meth-049.text: A prediction without an error bar is half an answer. Uncertainty quantification is the science of quantitatively characterising and estimating uncertainties in computational and real-world applications. It tries to determine how likely outcomes are when some aspects of a system are not exactly known. Forward propagation pushes input uncertainty through a model to get the output's mean and variance, its reliability or its full distribution. Forward methods include Monte Carlo simulation, surrogate models, local and functional expansions and first/second-order reliability methods. Inverse quantification estimates the discrepancy between model and experiment, and unknown parameters. Inverse problems are harder. They face dimensionality and identifiability issues, since different parameter and discrepancy combinations can give the same prediction.

soil-meth-033.title: Chemometrics: mining chemical measurements for answers
soil-meth-033.text: Svante Wold coined the word chemometrics in a 1971 grant application, and the field emerged in the 1970s as computers came into scientific use. It is the science of extracting information from chemical systems by data-driven means. It draws on multivariate statistics, applied mathematics and computer science to solve problems in chemistry, biology, medicine and engineering. Its natural material is spectra such as those from {{ref:soil-meth-013}}. Infrared and UV/visible spectra contain thousands of measurements per sample, but strong low-rank structure lets principal components analysis and partial least squares model them compactly. Models are usually judged by root mean squared error of prediction, and model selection relies on resampling such as bootstrap, permutation and cross-validation.

soil-meth-042.title: Partial least squares regression
soil-meth-042.text: When a spectrum has more wavelengths than a lab has samples, ordinary regression fails. Partial least squares (PLS) regression is built for exactly that case. It is a reduced-rank method that projects both predictors and responses into new spaces to find the relation between them. It looks for the direction in predictor space that explains maximum variance in response space, modelling the covariance structure of two matrices with latent variables. It suits data with more variables than observations, or with multicollinearity among predictors, where standard regression fails unless regularised. Components are extracted iteratively by finding directions of maximal covariance and regressing on the scores. PLS1 handles a single response vector and PLS-DA a categorical one. Herman Wold introduced it, with his son Svante Wold, first in the social sciences, and it is now most widely used in the field described in {{ref:soil-meth-033}}.

soil-meth-034.title: Multivariate calibration: turning spectra into soil properties
soil-meth-034.text: A near-infrared scan takes seconds, while a lab analysis can take days. Multivariate calibration closes the gap by building models that predict a property of interest from measured responses such as spectra. It draws on {{ref:soil-meth-033}} and is often applied to {{ref:soil-meth-013}}. A training set pairs reference values, for example analyte concentration, with the measured spectra. Partial least squares or principal component regression then relates response to property. Methods are classed as classical, which optimally describe the measured responses, or inverse, which need less physical knowledge and usually predict better in mean-squared-error terms. The payoff is that fast, cheap, non-destructive measurements can estimate properties that would otherwise need slow or costly analysis, even under heavy interference from other analytes. Broad, non-selective spectra can still predict properties when paired with careful calibration, because selectivity comes partly from the mathematics.

soil-env-111.title: Managing soil carbon: stop the losses, build the stock
soil-env-111.text:
Exchange of carbon between soils and the atmosphere is a significant part of the global carbon cycle, and humans and farming now affect it most. Managing soil carbon means choosing land and farm practices to avoid losses of soil organic carbon, covered in {{ref:soil-env-108}}, and to build it up.

Losses come from several directions. Land-use change such as deforestation has caused substantial soil carbon losses, though exact amounts are hard to measure. Fire strips soil cover and causes immediate and continuing losses. Tillage, described in {{ref:soil-agri-095}}, and drainage expose organic matter to oxygen, and peatlands in the Netherlands, East Anglia, Florida and the California Delta have subsided severely as a result. Grazing that leaves soil bare, through too long or too short recovery periods, also loses carbon.

Building carbon is not simple, because soil organisms consume and release carbon and become more active when nitrogen fertilizer is added. Still, past losses mean farmed soils can store more. Reducing tillage intensity and summer fallow cuts losses, while manure, biochar, cover crops, residue retention, perennials and good fertilization raise inputs. Farmers are discouraged from stubble burning and over-cultivation and encouraged to work in organic material such as manure.

soil-env-322.title: Climate tipping points
soil-env-322.text: A small push can sometimes cause a very large change. A climate tipping point is a critical threshold that, when crossed, leads to large, accelerating and often irreversible changes in the climate system. Self-reinforcing feedbacks, as in {{ref:soil-env-213}}, can make the change irreversible on a human timescale. Thawing permafrost releasing methane and melting ice sheets lowering albedo are examples, and crossing one threshold can trigger another in cascading tipping points. Three types are recognized: bifurcation-induced, noise-induced and rate-induced tipping. Only bifurcation-induced tipping shows early warning signals such as critical slowing down and rising autocorrelation and variance. Early IPCC assessments held tipping points likely only at about 4 degC or more of warming above preindustrial.

soil-env-324.title: Compost bomb instability in peatlands
soil-env-324.text: A peatland can sit quietly for years and then release its carbon all at once. This is rate-induced tipping, which occurs when an environmental change is faster than the force restoring the system to its stable state. In peatlands, after years of relative stability, it can produce an explosive release of soil carbon to the atmosphere. The phenomenon is sometimes called compost bomb instability. Peatland carbon is the subject of {{ref:soil-water-138}}.

soil-env-323.title: Permafrost thaw and its tipping dynamics
soil-env-323.text: Permafrost holds nearly twice as much carbon as the atmosphere. When it thaws, microbes decompose the newly unfrozen organic matter and release CO2 and methane, a self-reinforcing feedback. Most thaw is gradual over centuries, and the process is not expected to cause a global tipping point. Ice-rich permafrost is the exception. It can thaw abruptly, slumping or forming thermokarst lakes over years to decades, and these self-sustaining local dynamics could raise greenhouse gas emissions by around 40%. The frozen ground itself is described in {{ref:soil-env-129}}.

soil-env-325.title: The Cuvette Centrale peatland in the Congo Basin
soil-env-325.text:
Found in 2017, the Cuvette Centrale in the Congo Basin is the most vulnerable store of tropical peat carbon in the world, a kind of soil described in {{ref:soil-class-081}}.

Its size is striking. It holds about 30 petagrams of carbon, 28% of all tropical peat carbon. That equals all the trees in the other 96% of the Congo Basin, even though the peatland covers only 4%. Burning all of it would release the equivalent of three years of all anthropogenic CO2 emissions.

Protection is thin. Only 8% of this peat carbon lies within existing protected areas, while 26% is open to logging, mining or palm oil.

The climate adds to the risk. It is already drier than that of other tropical peatlands, and conditions 7,500 to 2,000 years ago were dry enough to release substantial peat. For that reason the Cuvette Centrale could become a climate tipping point, of the kind described in {{ref:soil-env-322}}.

soil-env-321.title: How compaction stunts roots
soil-env-321.text: Compaction removes large pores and raises penetration resistance, restricting roots and the organisms that live in soil. The large pores between aggregates go first. That hurts fine and medium soils most, because they depend on those pores for infiltration, percolation and air exchange, while coarse soils suffer less. Compacted soil also hardens as it dries, since many small pores hold water under high suction. A good soil keeps penetration resistance below the 300 psi (2 MPa) level at which root growth ceases, but compacted soil quickly exceeds it. Growing roots need pores wider than about 0.1 mm, the size of most root tips. Without them roots stay short and thick, with few fine roots or root hairs, and take up water and nutrients poorly. Roots meeting a mechanical barrier also send a hormonal signal that slows shoot growth, an effect hard to separate from drought. Subsoil compaction limits deep rooting and raises drought losses in rain-fed farming. Earthworms, insects and aerobic microbes need large pores and air exchange, so compacted soils hold fewer of them, though they return quickly once better practices are adopted. The process itself is described in {{ref:soil-phys-082}}.
